title: Lists
description: Store many values in one variable, pick them out, change them and loop over them.

blocks.text: A list stores several values in order, inside square brackets [ ] and separated by commas.

blocks.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]
print(fruits)
explanation: fruits is one variable holding three strings.
Printing a list shows the brackets and quotes too.

blocks.text: A list can hold numbers, text, True/False — or be empty. len() tells you how many items it has.

blocks.code:
marks = [72, 95, 48]
empty = []
mixed = ["Asha", 21, True]
print(len(marks))
print(len(empty))
print(mixed)
explanation: marks has 3 items.
[] is an empty list with 0 items.
One list can mix different types.

blocks.text: The word in checks whether a value is somewhere in a list. The answer is True or False.

blocks.code:
colours = ["red", "green", "blue"]
print("green" in colours)
print("pink" in colours)

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Forgetting a comma. ["a" "b"] is a list with ONE item, "ab", because Python joins strings that sit next to each other.
Lists keep items in the order you put them in.

questions.explanation: Lists use square brackets. Quotes make one string, and curly or round brackets make other kinds of collections.
len() counts items, not their total. There are 3 numbers in the list.
"cow" is not one of the items, so in gives False. It's not an error to check for a missing value.

questions.prompt: This list has 2 items, not 3. Why?
options: Strings in lists need single quotes
A comma is missing between "Asha" and "Ravi"
questions.explanation: Without the comma Python joins the two strings into "AshaRavi". Both single and double quotes work in lists.

subLevels.title: Indexing and slicing
subLevels.summary: Get, change and cut out items by position.

blocks.text: Every item has a position number called an index. The first index is 0, not 1.

blocks.code:
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
print(letters[0])
print(letters[2])
explanation: letters[0] is the first item.
letters[2] is the third item.

blocks.text: Negative indexes count from the end: -1 is the last item, -2 the one before it.

blocks.code:
letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d"]
print(letters[-1])
print(letters[-2])

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: letters[-1] always gives the last item, however long the list is.

blocks.code:
scores = [10, 20, 30]
scores[1] = 25
print(scores)
explanation: scores[1] is the second item.
Assigning to it replaces 20 with 25.

blocks.text: You can read AND change list items by index.
A slice list[start:stop] gives a new list from start up to, but not including, stop. Leave out start to begin at 0; leave out stop to go to the end.

blocks.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
print(nums[1:3])
print(nums[:2])
print(nums[3:])
explanation: nums[1:3] takes index 1 and 2.
nums[:2] takes the first two.
nums[3:] takes everything from index 3 to the end.

blocks.code:
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
print(days[3])
blocks.output: IndexError: list index out of range
explanation: The list has 3 items, so the indexes are 0, 1 and 2.
There is no index 3.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Using the length as an index. The last index is always len(list) - 1.

questions.explanation: Indexes start at 0, so x[1] is the second item. red would be x[0].
-1 means the last item. Negative indexes are allowed, so there is no error.
x[1:4] starts at index 1 (the value 2) and stops before index 4, so the 5 at index 4 is left out.

options: An IndexError, because the last index is 1
questions.explanation: Two items means indexes 0 and 1. Asking for items[2] goes past the end.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank to get the first three items: nums[____]
questions.explanation: A slice stops before the stop index, so :3 gives indexes 0, 1, 2. 1:3 would skip the first item.
a[0] = 9 replaces the first item. It doesn't insert a new one, so the list still has 3 items.

subLevels.title: List methods
subLevels.summary: append, insert, remove, pop, sort — plus max, min and sum.

blocks.text: A method is a function that belongs to a value. You call it with a dot: list.method().

blocks.code:
cart = ["milk"]
cart.append("bread")
cart.append("eggs")
print(cart)
explanation: append() adds one item to the end of the list.
The list itself is changed.

pages.title: Adding at a position with insert()

blocks.code:
queue = ["Asha", "Ravi"]
queue.insert(0, "Meera")
print(queue)
explanation: insert(index, value) puts the value at that index.
Everything after it moves one place along.

blocks.code:
tasks = ["wash", "cook", "study"]
tasks.remove("cook")
print(tasks)
last = tasks.pop()
print(last)
print(tasks)
explanation: remove() deletes the first item equal to the value you give.
pop() removes the last item AND gives it back, so you can store it.

blocks.code:
marks = [72, 95, 48, 66]
marks.sort()
print(marks)
marks.sort(reverse=True)
print(marks)
explanation: sort() puts the items in order, smallest first.
reverse=True sorts largest first.

blocks.text: These built-in functions work on a whole list of numbers. Together they make quick statistics.

blocks.code:
marks = [72, 95, 48, 66, 81]
marks.append(73)
print(max(marks))
print(min(marks))
print(sum(marks) / len(marks))
explanation: max() gives the biggest value, min() the smallest.
sum() adds everything up: 435.
Dividing by len() (6 marks) gives the average.

blocks.text: Methods like append() and sort() change the list itself. They don't give back a new list — they give back None.

blocks.code:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
nums = nums.sort()
print(nums)
explanation: nums.sort() sorts the list and returns None.
nums = ... then replaces the sorted list with None.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Writing nums = nums.sort(). Just call nums.sort() on its own line.

items: insert(i, x) — add at index i
pop() — remove and return the last item
count(x) — how many times x appears

questions.explanation: append() adds the value to the end of the list, not the start.
sort() orders the list smallest first. Here the list is printed after sorting, so it isn't None.

questions.prompt: What does pop() do when you give it no index?
options: Adds an item at the end
Removes the last item and returns it
questions.explanation: pop() takes from the end by default and hands the item back. remove() is the one that deletes by value.

options: sort() changes the list in place and returns None
Lists of numbers can't be sorted
questions.explanation: x = x.sort() stores sort()'s return value, which is None. Call x.sort() on its own instead.
sum is 60 and len is 3. Dividing with / always gives a float, so it shows 20.0, not 20.

subLevels.title: Looping over lists
subLevels.summary: Visit every item with a for loop.

blocks.text: A for loop can walk through a list directly. The loop variable takes each item in turn.

blocks.output:
I like apple
I like banana
I like mango

blocks.code:
prices = [40, 25, 60]
total = 0
for price in prices:
    total += price
print(total)
explanation: price is 40, then 25, then 60.
The same add-up pattern you used with range().

blocks.text: Combine a loop, an if and append() to pick out the items you want.

explanation: passed starts empty.
Only marks of 50 or more are added.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Writing for m in range(marks). range() needs a number, not a list — loop over the list itself with for m in marks.
for x in my_list visits every item, in order.

questions.explanation: The loop prints each item on its own line. It loops over the items, not their index numbers.
The numbers are added: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12. They are numbers, not strings, so they aren't joined into 246.
questions.code:
total = 0
for n in [2, 4, 6]:
    total += n
print(total)

questions.prompt: Which is a correct way to loop over the list names?
questions.explanation: Loop over the list directly. range() needs a number, so range(names) is a TypeError.
Only numbers greater than 4 are appended. The new list is printed, not how many items it has.

subLevels.title: List comprehensions
subLevels.summary: Build a new list in one line (the simple way).

blocks.text: Here is the loop-and-append pattern you already know:

blocks.code:
squares = []
for n in range(1, 5):
    squares.append(n * n)
print(squares)

blocks.text: A list comprehension does the same thing in one line:

blocks.code:
squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 5)]
print(squares)
explanation: Read it as: "n * n for each n in range(1, 5)".
The result is a brand-new list.

items: what_to_keep — the value that goes into the new list
for name in source — the same as a normal for loop

blocks.code:
names = ["asha", "ravi"]
loud = [name + "!" for name in names]
print(loud)

blocks.text: Put an if at the end to keep only some items.

blocks.code:
marks = [35, 80, 52, 91]
passed = [m for m in marks if m >= 50]
print(passed)
explanation: Same result as the loop in 5.4, in one line.
Only items where the if is True are kept.

blocks.text: A list comprehension always makes a new list. The original list is not changed.

blocks.code:
prices = [100, 250, 80]
with_tax = [p + 10 for p in prices]
print(with_tax)
print(prices)

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Putting the parts in the wrong order, like [for p in prices p + 10]. The value always comes first, then for.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: If a comprehension gets hard to read, use a normal loop. Both are correct.

questions.explanation: range(3) gives 0, 1, 2, and each is doubled. It starts at 0, so the first value is 0, not 2.
Only items where x > 2 is True are kept, and the items themselves go in the list, not True/False.
questions.code: print([x for x in [1, 2, 3, 4] if x > 2])

questions.prompt: Which loop does [w + "s" for w in words] replace?
options: A for loop that appends w + "s" to a new list for each w in words
A while loop that removes items from words
A for loop that prints each word
questions.explanation: A comprehension builds a new list from a for loop. It doesn't print or change the original list.

options: The colon should be a semicolon
The value must come first: [n * 2 for n in nums]
questions.explanation: A comprehension is written [value for name in source], with no colon. Square brackets are correct.
Each word is joined with itself, giving one new item per word in a list.
questions.code:
words = ["hi", "yo"]
print([w + w for w in words])

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank to keep only even numbers.
questions.explanation: A filter uses if at the end. n % 2 == 1 would keep the odd numbers instead.

options: A list comprehension changes the original list
A list comprehension can only use range()
A list comprehension prints each item
A list comprehension always creates a new list
questions.explanation: The source list stays the same. You can loop over any list, not just range().
2 is skipped by the filter, and the kept numbers are multiplied by 10.
questions.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
result = [n * 10 for n in nums if n != 2]
print(result)
